newsitem.title: INDIA: Sikh-Hindu team wins big majority in India Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Sikh-Hindu team wins big majority in India Punjab.

text.p: A Sikh-Hindu alliance in India's northern state of Punjab has won an overwhelming majority in peaceful local elections, officials said on Monday.

They said the pro-Sikh Akali Dal Party had won 68 seats in Friday's polls and its rightwing Hindu nationalist ally, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had taken 18 with 108 results declared in the 117-member state assembly.
"This is a sweeping victory, a good result from unprecedented peaceful polls," Punjab's chief electoral officer, Brajendra Singh, told Reuters.

The Congress party, which won 87 seats in the last assembly polls in 1992, took 12 this time and was not expected to add many more. The Communist Party of India and the low-caste Bahujan Samaj Party won one seat each.
A pro-separatist faction of the Akali Dal won one seat.
Congress swept to power in the 1992 elections at the end of a decade-long Sikh separatist war. But voting was then held in an atmosphere of fear and violence despite a crackdown on militancy.
Singh said the Akali Dal and the BJP, India's main opposition party, were ahead in most of the nine constituencies where votes were still being counted.

The separatist rebellion in the rich farming state bordering Pakistan peaked in June 1984 when India sent troops into the Golden Temple, Sikhism's holiest shrine, in Amristar to flush out armed guerrillas.
In October that year, prime minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead by two of her own Sikh bodyguards, apparently in revenge for the army action in the Golden Temple.
Elections in 1992 brought back peace to Punjab. At the peak of the insurgency the Akali Dal was considered to be sympathetic to separatist militants.
